- If sentiment is consistently low (≤0.3) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast by 2–5%.
- If sentiment spikes (≥0.7) followed by a sharp price drop, model often overshoots the dip; cap forecast at 1–2% below recent low.
- When model forecasts a sharp upward move after a recent dip, check for mean reversion; if sentiment is neutral or slightly positive, cap forecast at 1–3% below peak.
- If model consistently forecasts higher than true outcome in 3–5 consecutive days, apply downward bias correction (−1.5% to −3% per day).
- If sentiment is high (≥0.7) and model forecasts are low, model underestimates; increase forecast by 1–3% to align with sentiment momentum.
- For 30-day forecasts, if true outcome deviates >5% from 14-day moving average, adjust forecast to align with recent trend (not just historical mean).
- If sentiment is volatile (fluctuating >0.3) and model is averaging, reduce forecast smoothing; use sentiment-weighted moving average for correction.
- If model forecasts a sharp peak followed by a steep decline, check for lag: true outcome often lags 1–3 days; adjust forecast to reflect 1–3 day delay in peak.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.2) and model forecasts are high, reduce forecast by 3–5% to reflect bearish sentiment.
- If model forecasts are consistently 2–4% above true outcome, apply downward correction (−2% to −4%) for next 3–5 days, especially if sentiment is neutral or negative.
